- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.7) and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid overreaction.  
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.3) and forecast is overly conservative, slightly increase the low-end of the range to avoid premature bottoming.  
- After a strong upward move in history, model tends to overestimate continuation; apply a 3–5 day lag correction to peak forecasts.  
- When sentiment swings sharply (e.g., from 0.3 to 0.8), model often misjudges direction; align forecast slope with sentiment momentum rather than historical trend.  
- For 30-day horizons, mean reversion bias is common after 2–3 consecutive spikes; apply a 1–2% downward adjustment to forecasted peaks.  
- If sentiment is neutral (0.3–0.7) and forecast is volatile, smooth out extremes by averaging 3–5 consecutive forecast points.  
- Overshoots after sentiment spikes (e.g., +10% above recent high) should be capped at +5% to prevent overcorrection.  
- When sentiment is negative and price is near recent low, avoid forecasting further decline; instead, project slight rebound if sentiment recovers.
